org.metaDescription: {org.name} at {parent.shortName} — research and design for better learning across the lifespan.

hero.headline: Learning sciences and technology across the lifespan
hero.summary: Advancing rigorous research and design for better learning from K-12 through higher education, professional life, and the third age — grounded in the realities of India and the Global South while contributing to the global research community.

vision.heading: Vision
vision.value: A future in which every learner — from childhood through higher education, professional life, and the third age — has access to adaptive, engaging, and equitable learning experiences that are grounded in the science of how people learn.
alternatives: A future in which every learner — from school through higher education, professional life, and the third age — has access to adaptive, engaging, and equitable learning experiences that are grounded in the science of how people learn.

mission.heading: Mission
mission.value: The {org.name} ({org.shortName}) at {parent.shortName} advances rigorous research and design at the intersection of learning sciences, artificial intelligence, and educational technology. We focus on four domains across the lifespan — K-12 education, higher education, flexible learning for working professionals and executives, and third-age learning — developing solutions that are effective, inclusive, and scalable for India and the Global South, while contributing foundational knowledge to the global research community.

approach.heading: Our Approach
approach.intro: We combine the learning sciences with technology design and open infrastructure. Research is organised around four fundamental questions that apply across the lifespan:
approach.outro: At the heart of our work is the Learning Middleware — an open technology layer that makes the tools of learning sciences available to educators, researchers, and institutions across all four domains.

whyIiith.heading: Why {parent.shortName}
whyIiith.value: {parent.shortName} is structured around research centres rather than traditional departments. This model enables deep interdisciplinary work. {org.shortName} builds on the institute’s strengths in artificial intelligence, human-computer interaction, language technologies, and flexible learning, while focusing these capabilities on the science and design of learning across the lifespan.

domains.title: K-12 Education
domains.summary: Designing the future of school learning in the age of AI, grounded in the realities of Indian classrooms and systems.
context: In the age of AI, Indian K-12 education confronts four fundamental questions: What should students learn? How should teachers teach? How do students learn most effectively? And how should learning be evaluated?

{org.shortName} designs and studies technology-enabled interventions that address these questions with scientific rigor and practical relevance. Our work is rooted in the distinctive conditions of Indian schooling — multilingual classrooms, large public systems, teacher capacity constraints, foundational literacy and numeracy priorities, and the ambitions of NEP 2020 — while generating knowledge that advances the global learning sciences.

questions.heading: What students should learn
questions.body: Curriculum frameworks, learning progressions, and competency models that balance foundational knowledge with the capabilities required in an AI era: critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, digital and AI literacy, creativity, and ethical reasoning — developed for Indian languages and contexts.

questions.heading: How teachers should teach
questions.body: AI-supported and human-centered pedagogical tools and practices that amplify teacher expertise. This includes intelligent orchestration systems, classroom analytics, and professional learning models that work at scale in real Indian schools.

questions.heading: How students learn
questions.body: Adaptive learning environments, multilingual tools, and scaffolds that promote deeper understanding, self-regulated learning, and learner agency. Research examines how students actually interact with these systems in classroom and home settings.

questions.heading: How learning is evaluated
questions.body: Next-generation assessment approaches that remain valid when AI can generate traditional answers — formative systems, process data, authentic tasks, and feedback mechanisms that support both equity and continuous improvement.

domains.title: Higher Education
domains.summary: Redesigning teaching, learning, and assessment in universities and colleges for an AI-transformed world.
context: Indian higher education is being reshaped by generative AI, massification, and the demand for graduates who can thrive in an AI-shaped economy. Faculty, academic leaders, and institutions need rigorous guidance on what to teach, how to teach, how students learn, and how learning should be evaluated.

{org.shortName} designs and studies technology-enabled interventions that answer these questions. Our work engages the distinctive features of Indian higher education — large-enrolment courses, diverse student preparedness, multilingual contexts, and the push for flexible, multidisciplinary curricula under NEP 2020 — while contributing evidence to the international research community.

questions.heading: What students should learn
questions.body: Programme and course designs that integrate disciplinary depth with AI-era competencies: critical and ethical use of AI, research and inquiry skills, interdisciplinary problem-solving, and professional readiness.

questions.heading: How faculty should teach
questions.body: AI-supported instructional models and faculty development approaches for both large-enrolment and specialised courses. We develop tools and pedagogies that preserve the essential role of the teacher while amplifying reach and impact.

questions.heading: How students learn
questions.body: Adaptive courseware, learning analytics, and collaborative environments that support self-regulated learning, conceptual understanding, and productive engagement with generative AI.

questions.heading: How learning is evaluated
questions.body: Assessment approaches that remain meaningful in an AI era — authentic and performance-based tasks, process-oriented evaluation, competency-based systems, and analytics that provide timely feedback while supporting equity and student success.

domains.title: Flexible Learning for Professionals & Executives
domains.summary: Designing adaptive, high-impact continuous learning that fits the realities of work and leadership.
context: Working professionals and executives must learn continuously as AI reshapes jobs, industries, and leadership itself. Organisations and learners need evidence-based answers to what professionals should learn, how learning should be designed, how adults learn most effectively under real constraints, and how progress and impact should be evaluated.

{org.shortName} designs and studies technology-enabled interventions that address these questions. Our work is grounded in the Indian and Global South context of rapid digital transformation, large and diverse workforces, and the growing demand for high-quality, scalable professional and executive development.

questions.heading: What professionals should learn
questions.body: Capabilities required in an AI-transformed workplace: AI literacy and fluency, domain-specific continuous learning, adaptive leadership, collaboration with intelligent systems, and ethical decision-making.

questions.heading: How learning should be designed and facilitated
questions.body: Flexible, modular, and work-integrated architectures — micro-learning, cohort-based programmes, AI-supported coaching, and platforms that embed learning in the flow of work — designed for the time and motivation realities of adult learners.

questions.heading: How professionals learn
questions.body: Self-directed and adaptive pathways, social and peer learning, and productive integration of AI tools, grounded in adult learning theory and real workplace contexts.

questions.heading: How progress and impact are evaluated
questions.body: Approaches suited to professional learning: demonstration of competence, transfer to workplace performance, micro-credentials, continuous feedback, and measures of individual and organisational value.

domains.title: Third-Age Learning
domains.summary: Enabling older adults to continue learning, connecting, and participating fully through thoughtfully designed technology-supported experiences.
context: As populations age and digital technologies become central to daily life, older adults face both new opportunities and barriers to continued learning. Families, community organisations, and older learners themselves need guidance on what is worth learning in later life, how learning should be supported, how older adults learn most effectively, and how progress and benefit should be understood.

{org.shortName} designs and studies technology-enabled interventions that address these questions with rigor and respect. Our work is rooted in Indian and Global South realities — demographic ageing, intergenerational families, uneven digital access, and the need for culturally resonant, low-barrier solutions — while contributing to the global knowledge base on lifelong learning and active ageing.

questions.heading: What is worth learning
questions.body: Opportunities that matter in later life: digital and AI literacy for everyday participation, cognitive engagement, health and financial literacy, creative expression, intergenerational knowledge sharing, and personal growth — designed for meaning and dignity.

questions.heading: How learning is supported
questions.body: Age-friendly architectures: accessible platforms, community-based and intergenerational models, facilitated group learning, and gentle AI support that prioritise clarity, social presence, and respect for life experience.

questions.heading: How older adults learn
questions.body: Motivation and meaning-making, social learning, adaptation to technology, and strategies that accommodate possible changes in cognition or digital familiarity, studied in real community and family settings.

questions.heading: How progress and benefit are understood
questions.body: Evaluation focused on sustained engagement, sense of competence and connection, cognitive and social benefits, digital confidence, and contribution to well-being — rather than traditional high-stakes assessment.

roadmap.heading: Roadmap
roadmap.intro: As a new centre, we are deliberately transparent about our growth path:

phases.title: Foundation
phases.body: Establish core team, launch the website and brand, define priority research themes, begin seed projects, and open collaboration pathways.

phases.title: Momentum
phases.body: Produce early research outputs, pilot interventions, grow the team, advance the Learning Middleware toward open release, and establish first international and national partnerships.

phases.title: Scale & Impact
phases.body: Expand across all four pillars, release open infrastructure, develop professional learning programmes, and demonstrate measurable impact with education systems and organisations.

platform.name: Learning Middleware
platform.summary: An open technology layer designed to make the tools of learning sciences available to educators, researchers, and institutions across the entire spectrum of learners. By releasing it as open source, we aim to lower barriers and accelerate evidence-based innovation for K-12, higher education, professional learning, and third-age contexts.
description: A good deal of serious work in the learning sciences never leaves the project that produced it. The Learning Middleware is an open technology layer so that teachers, faculty, institutions, and researchers can actually use those methods.

It will be released as open source. This is not a platform for its own sake. It is a way to lower the cost of doing evidence-based work, and to make the Centre’s research usable beyond {parent.shortName}.
The middleware is intended to support work across schools, colleges and universities, professional and executive learning, and later life.
audiences: Researchers in learning sciences and educational technology
platform.statusText: The middleware has been conceptualised and is being developed toward a general, open-source release. Detailed architecture, documentation, and early-adopter pathways will be published as the work matures.

people.name: Prof. Raj Reddy
people.headline: Moza Bint Nasser University Professor of Computer Science and Robotics, Carnegie Mellon University
subtitleLines: Moza Bint Nasser University Professor of Computer Science and Robotics, Carnegie Mellon University
people.bioShort: Dabbala Rajagopal "Raj" Reddy is an Indian-American computer scientist and one of the early pioneers of artificial intelligence. He serves as the Chief Mentor for {org.shortName}, guiding its research and vision at the intersection of AI and education. He and Edward Feigenbaum won the 1994 ACM Turing Award for their pioneering work in artificial intelligence.
people.bio: Dabbala Rajagopal "Raj" Reddy is an Indian-American computer scientist and one of the early pioneers of artificial intelligence. He has served on the faculty of Stanford and Carnegie Mellon for over 50 years and was the founding director of the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. As the founding chairman of the {parent.name} ({parent.abbreviation}), he has been instrumental in shaping the institution's vision. He and Edward Feigenbaum won the 1994 ACM Turing Award for their pioneering work in artificial intelligence. He serves as the Chief Mentor for {org.shortName}, guiding its research and vision at the intersection of AI and education.

people.name: Ashok K. Goel
people.headline: Professor of Computer Science and Human-Centered Computing, Georgia Institute of Technology
subtitleLines: Executive Director, NSF National AI Institute for Adult Learning and Online Education
Chief Scientist, Center for 21st Century Universities
people.bio: Ashok Goel works at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and learning. For more than a decade his research has focused on AI in education and education in AI. His laboratory created Jill Watson, among the first virtual teaching assistants used at scale in online higher education, and he leads the US National Science Foundation’s AI Institute for Adult Learning and Online Education. A Fellow of AAAI and the Cognitive Science Society, he received AAAI’s Outstanding AI Educator Award. He advises {org.shortName} on how AI can support teaching presence, adult and online learning, and institute-scale experimentation rather than one-off tools.

people.name: Ryan S. Baker
people.headline: Professor of Artificial Intelligence and Education, Adelaide University
subtitleLines: Director, Penn Center for Learning Analytics
Adjunct Professor, University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education
people.bio: Ryan Baker uses educational data mining and learning analytics to study how students actually use digital learning environments — and what that use predicts. He has built models of engagement, affect, and “gaming the system” across intelligent tutors, games, and MOOCs, and developed the BROMP classroom observation protocol used by researchers in several countries. Founding president of the International Educational Data Mining Society and Associate Editor of the Journal of Educational Data Mining, he teaches the long-running MOOC Big Data and Education. He advises {org.shortName} on evidence, measurement, and the responsible use of learner data across K-12 and higher education.

people.name: Matthew Kam
people.headline: Former Employee of Google
subtitleLines: Former Staff User Experience Researcher, Software Engineering Education
people.bio: Matthew Kam studies how learning technologies are designed and used at scale, and how AI is changing the work people must learn to do. At Google he led research that shaped products used by more than 100 million students and teachers, including Chromebooks in education, Google Classroom, Google Forms, and Expeditions. His earlier academic work at UC Berkeley and Carnegie Mellon designed mobile literacy games with children in rural and low-income schools in India. He advises organizations including Google.org, UNICEF, and the Computing Research Association. For {org.shortName} he brings human-centered product research, workforce-relevant AI learning, and design for large, diverse school systems.

people.name: J. Derek Lomas
people.headline: Professor of Positive AI, Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering, TU Delft
subtitleLines: Cofounder, Playpower Labs and Smart Paper
people.bio: Derek Lomas designs AI systems that support learning and wellbeing, not only efficiency. Trained in cognitive science (Yale), design (UC San Diego), and HCI (Carnegie Mellon, with Ken Koedinger and Jodi Forlizzi), he used large-scale experiments to optimize educational games for motivation and learning. Through Playpower Labs and Smart Paper he has reached millions of learners; Smart Paper’s computer-vision assessment of paper work has been used in 65,000 schools in India, reaching 4.7 million students. He advises {org.shortName} on learning-experience design, AI at classroom scale in Indian contexts, and keeping human judgement at the centre of automated systems.

people.name: Vasudeva Varma
people.headline: Professor at {parent.shortName}
people.bio: Vasudeva Varma is a Professor and the Head of the {org.name} ({org.shortName}) at {parent.shortName}. He previously served as the Dean of Research and Development and CEO of {parent.shortName}. His research focuses on Information Retrieval, Extraction, and Access, with specific interests in Social Media Analysis, Semantic Search, and Text Generation. He is a recipient of the Google Research Award for his work in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.

people.name: Praveen Garimella
people.headline: Associate Professor of Practice
people.bio: Praveen Garimella is an educational technology practitioner, learning scientist, and systems architect. He serves as an Associate Professor of Practice at {org.shortName}, {parent.shortName}, and as an Adjunct Faculty member in the Software & Societal Systems Department at Carnegie Mellon University. With over two decades of experience at the intersection of cognitive science, AI, and platform engineering, he focuses on designing intelligent tutoring systems and mastery-based learning ecosystems.

people.name: Dr. Santanu Paul
people.headline: Adjunct Faculty
people.bio: Dr. Santanu Paul is the founding CEO and Managing Director of TalentSprint. He has served as Senior Vice President for Global Delivery Operations at Virtusa Corporation. He holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, and a B.Tech. in Computer Science from IIT Madras. He is a Visiting Professor at IIT Hyderabad and serves on the boards of organizations such as NPCI and NSDL Payments Bank.

people.name: Dr. Vamshi Ambati
people.headline: Adjunct Faculty
people.bio: Dr. Vamshi Ambati is an AI entrepreneur, researcher, and investor. He earned his Ph.D. from the Language Technologies Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. He has founded multiple companies, including LatentStructure and Predera, and has held technical roles at PayPal and Base CRM. He is currently an investor at Virama Ventures.

background.heading: Background
paragraphs: AI systems can now complete much of routine schoolwork, undergraduate assignments and office work. An AI system completing a task is no evidence that the person who submitted it has learned anything. Homework is being finished in minutes, and children ask, reasonably, why they should avoid a tool that already holds the answer.

Prohibition fails, because students will use these tools anyway. Removing all friction fails for a different reason. Understanding usually arrives just before a student succeeds, and a tool that steps in at that moment improves the submitted work while taking away the learning. The Centre works on the remaining case: AI used while learning, so the learner can still reason when the tool is absent.

event.heading: Inaugural

pressCoverage.prefix: About a hundred faculty, students, school leaders, edtech practitioners and friends of the Institute attended. R. Chandrashekhar, former President of NASSCOM, launched the Centre as Chief Guest. Prof. Raj Reddy, Chief Mentor to the Centre, addressed the gathering. National and local press covered the launch with enthusiasm, and the reports are collected at
pressCoverage.label: iiit.ac.in/iiit-h-launches-cetls

paragraphs: Vasudeva Varma, founding head of the Centre, presented the initiatives it begins with: tailored programmes for school teachers on AI literacy, profiling of learners and teachers on how they use AI, Silver Rooms for older adults, and the revised MSIT programme as the first study site in higher education.

Praveen Garimella ran two roundtables in the afternoon, one with school leaders and one with edtech companies working in K-12, on the most pressing challenges and openings for AI in schools. Both discussions are continuing.
event.questionsIntro: The speakers at the inaugural pointed the Centre towards three questions.
questions: The first is what should be taught, and how it should be assessed, when a capable assistant is always available. Prof. Reddy holds that much of the present curriculum is already on the web, and that classroom time should move towards judgement, particularly the ability to tell when an answer is wrong.

The second is whether learning outcomes can be raised at the same or lower public cost with the teacher retained as the central intermediary, given that outcomes in India are well below where they need to be, that the education budget will not double, and that students will use AI tools whether or not policy permits it. Mr Chandrashekhar asked that the Centre stay close to implementation, recalling an earlier digital-education programme in which infrastructure spending was not matched by content quality.

The third is the conditions under which AI assistance preserves or increases productive struggle, since early experimental reports associate heavy use of AI for writing and programming with signs of cognitive diminution and the conditions under which assistance helps have not been established.

programmeAreas.heading: Programme areas
programmeAreas.intro: The Centre tests interventions with real learners across the lifespan. Four areas are defined, and each will begin several initiatives of its own.

items.title: School education
items.body: Work will be carried out in schools with teachers, students and parents. Open questions include instruction in Indian languages, science and mathematics understood as well as answered, AI literacy for teachers before AI reaches children, and a workable path for board-level AI curricula. CBSE’s proposed AI education from Grade 1 to 12 is policy running ahead of evidence. A monthly dialogue among school stakeholders has been proposed, with a compiled note for state and central governments.

items.title: Higher education
items.body: The first engineering artefact is Learning Middleware (LMW), a software layer between AI models on one side and teachers and students on the other. The instructor-facing side supports the design of more learnable material, using the Knowledge, Learning and Instruction (KLI) framework from Carnegie Mellon’s LearnLab. The learner-facing side adapts to what a student knows and where they get stuck.

items.title: Workplace and continuing education
items.body: With the Division for Flexible Learning, the work extends to employed professionals and to independent and gig workers, through offerings from a few hours to full degrees taken outside a classroom. The research problem specific to this setting is signal loss. Online, the evidence of learning is often limited to what a learner types and where they click, and the Centre will study whether learning state can be inferred from such traces well enough for a distance course to match on-campus instruction.

items.title: Later-life (Third Age) learning
items.body: Because people live and work well beyond sixty, the Centre treats learning after retirement as a research area. A third-age learning research group, with colleagues from cognitive science, will study how older adults learn, including crystallised and fluid intelligence at that age. New North, recorded conversations with highly productive people in their seventies and beyond, continues. Silver Rooms, structured conversations on AI in daily life, online safety and ageing well, will develop into intergenerational programmes on campus.

advisersAndSupport.supportBody: More than a dozen faculty across the Institute are affiliated with the Centre, and the core faculty will grow to between eight and ten over two to three years. Hiring is open for faculty, postdoctoral researchers, doctoral students and learning engineers. The first founding donors committed within a day of being asked, and a small number of founding-supporter places remain open until the end of September 2026.

collaboratorsSought.heading: Collaborators sought
collaboratorsSought.body: The Centre is looking for school leaders who will permit sustained work in their schools as controlled studies, builders of learning tools willing to have them evaluated on learning outcomes, faculty and students from computing, cognitive science, language and design, and supporters of work that takes time to show results.
